question: Does Java automatically synthesize a copy constructor if a class does not declare one?

options.text: Yes, the compiler automatically generates a shallow copy constructor for every class.
Yes, but only if the class implements the Cloneable marker interface.
Yes, whenever the assignment operator = is used between two class variables.
No, Java never synthesizes a copy constructor; it must be written explicitly by the programmer.

explanation: Unlike C++, Java does not provide an implicit copy constructor. If a class requires a copy constructor, the developer must explicitly define one that accepts an instance of the class as a parameter.

question: What occurs when one object reference variable is assigned to another using b = a?

options.text: A deep recursive copy is performed across all fields of object a.
Only the reference memory address is copied, so both variables point to the same object.
The compiler invokes the default copy constructor of class type a.
A new distinct clone of object a is created on the heap and assigned to b.

explanation: Assignment between object reference variables in Java copies only the reference value (the heap pointer). Both variables become aliases pointing to the exact same object in memory.

question: Does defining a copy constructor in a Java class require implementing the Cloneable interface?

options.text: No, copy constructors are regular constructors and have no dependency on Cloneable.
No, provided the compiler automatically generated the default copy constructor first.
Yes, any class that duplicates objects must implement Cloneable to avoid compiler errors.
Yes, because copy constructors internally delegate to super.clone().

explanation: A copy constructor is simply an ordinary constructor that takes an instance of its own class type. It operates completely independently of the Cloneable interface and Object.clone().

question: In a copy constructor, what is the effect of directly assigning a mutable reference field with this.data = other.data?

options.text: It automatically triggers the Cloneable interface on the nested member object.
The compiler rejects the statement because fields cannot be copied directly.
It creates an independent deep copy of the mutable data object.
It creates a shallow copy where both the original and new objects share the same internal data object.

explanation: Directly assigning a reference field copies the pointer address, resulting in a shallow copy. Both instances will reference the same shared mutable object, so mutations through one instance will affect the other.
